newsitem.title: PERU: Fresh impasse shrouds Peru hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Fresh impasse shrouds Peru hostage crisis.

text.p: Peru's 81-day hostage crisis faced a new impasse on Saturday as President Alberto Fujimori stressed he wanted a peaceful outcome but Marxist rebels holding 72 men showed no sign of returning to the bargaining table.

In Tokyo, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Saturday urged the Peruvian government and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) to resume talks to end the siege at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.
"There is no benefit for either side in (the talks) remaining suspended," Hashimoto told reporters, but he had no idea when the talks might be restarted.
Police loudspeakers blasted traditional Peruvian waltzes early on Saturday at the besieged residence while heavy fog rolled in off the Pacific.

Rebel leader Nestor Cerpa abruptly called off Friday's scheduled face-to-face meeting with the government, charging security forces were digging tunnels to attack the diplomatic compound where rebels and their captives are holed up.
On Friday, mediators trying to resolve the siege peacefully also urged both sides to restart talks and Fujimori vowed he would use "a humanitarian sense" and seek a bloodless end to the crisis.
But the president dodged reporters' questions about the rebels' charges of a tunnel and left open the possibility of a violent solution if hostages are harmed.
In a statement, Fujimori said the bloodless path would be followed only as long as the MRTA "fully respected the life and health of the hostages."
"The state, in consequence, will stay alert at all times to any change in this scenario," the statement said.
But in a meeting on Friday, Fujimori assured members of a guarantors commission mediating the talks that he still wanted a peaceful outcome to Latin America's longest hostage crisis.
"We have received the express confirmation of this very same intention from the president in a meeting," Vatican representative Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani said in a statement read to reporters.
Cipriani, a member of the three-man mediating panel, noted that Fujimori and Hashimoto had agreed in Canada last month to seek a peaceful solution to the crisis and prevent loss of life.
Fujimori met with his negotiators on Friday to map their next move, meeting twice with his chief negotiator, Domingo Palermo.
Some progress had been made in the nine rounds of talks between the government and rebels since discussions restarted on Feb. 11, with both sides on Wednesday laying out formal proposals.
But the MRTA refused to attend the tenth round, set for Friday, dashing optimism for a peaceful solution and heightening tension in the standoff.
Peruvian officials, including Defence Minister Tomas Castillo Meza, denied the existence of the tunnels, but Lima newspapers were full of precise details of where and how they were being built.
One report, citing state sources, gave the address of the building where one tunnel supposedly began and said it would lead into the compound's kitchen or dining room.
The rebels have been holding the hostages, including Fujimori's brother, Pedro, and two cabinet ministers, since Dec. 17 in the diplomatic compound.

On Thursday, Cerpa said rebels had heard sounds coming from under the mansion's floor and charged the government aimed to rescue the hostages while he and his second-in-command, Rolly Rojas, attended talks at a safe house across the street from the diplomatic residence.

Security force sources consulted by Reuters confirmed that at least four tunnels had been dug under the compound in recent weeks. The tunnels would be used if there was an attack, which would last seven minutes and cause many deaths, they added.
